title: Christ Sings in Every Subject
author: Zach Howard
summary: Howard argues that the end of education is not information or skill but the formation of loves, and that delight and study feed each other in what he calls a positive flywheel. Reading Psalm 111:2 alongside C.S. Lewis on ordo amoris, he claims that students cannot value a subject until their affections have been trained, and that the teacher's own visible joy is the primary instrument of that training. The essay then turns to the problem every veteran teacher faces, namely the loss of delight in material rehearsed year after year. Drawing on Augustine's letter Instructing Beginners in Faith, Howard proposes that the remedy is not fresh content but redirected attention, moving from what is taught to whom it is taught. Compassion for the student, he contends, lets the teacher see a familiar truth again through a beginner's eyes, much as a local rediscovers a landmark while showing it to visitors. The piece closes by insisting that learning pursued for joy necessarily overflows outward into love of God and neighbor, so that delight, study and charity form a single circuit rather than competing aims.
points: Delight and study reinforce each other in a flywheel, so a teacher who wants durable learning has to work on the student's affections rather than only on content coverage.
Howard enlists Lewis and Augustine to argue that rightly ordered love is a trainable capacity, which makes the formation of taste a legitimate classroom objective.
External motivators such as grades and paychecks keep a classroom running but produce learning that stops the moment the last grade is posted.
Augustine's counsel for a bored teacher is to shift attention from the subject to the student, because compassion for a beginner revives the teacher's own sense of the material.
The essay treats teaching as reciprocal, with the student's first encounter restoring to the teacher a freshness that repetition had worn away.
quotes: We tend to study what delights us. When a delicious new flavor hits our taste buds, we ask for the secret ingredient.

Those who delight in God's many works of creation and redemption channel their delight into deeper study. If it is true that delight leads to study, then we should expect that, with worthy objects, further study leads to greater delight.
True education aims not merely at acquiring information or skills but at forming our souls' capacities for lasting joy.
Most people have experienced a boring classroom. The learning is lifeless. The study is all drudgery and no delight. Student and teacher alike count the minutes until class is over.
Good teachers lead their students to see what is honorable and lovely about their subject. But for the student to value what he studies, he needs more than information; his loves must be formed.
The teacher's joy in his subject invites the student to join him in delight. Learning that leads to joy will last far longer than the hour in the classroom.
Augustine guides us to shift our attention from what we are teaching to whom we are teaching. When our subject no longer excites us, he says, we must draw near to the student with love.

In our teaching, we have the distinct privilege of reviving our joy in familiar truths through the delight of our students encountering them for the first time. The familiar becomes fresh when we see through their eyes.
